#341. Best Wireless Earbuds I’d Buy Right Now (2026): Apple, Beats, Bose, and More

I use Wireless earbuds constantly. I use them for work, running, working out, relaxing, traveling—whatever I am doing, chances are I have a pair of wireless earbuds on me, just in case. While some of the earliest models were huge and inconvenient, earbuds nowadays are slim, comfortable, and often affordable.

But I don’t just use earbuds—I test them. Hundreds of them, actually. After weeks of music, calls, commutes, and rogue earbuds flying out of my ears, I’ve chosen these favorites as the best for most people.

For more top picks, check out WIRED’s other audio guides, like the Best Open Earbuds, Best Noise-Canceling Earbuds, and Best Workout Headphones.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Updated November 2026: I’ve updated our best overall pick and added new honorable mentions and other earbuds tested. I’ve also updated specs, prices, and links.

The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro are the best earbuds for most people because of their showstopping call quality, excellent noise-canceling, and reasonable $170 price tag. I was frankly floored when I tested their microphone quality against pricier Apple, Bose, and Sony earbuds—the Liberty 5 Pro mopped the floor with them. A bustling cafe, a city street full of traffic, a highway overpass—everyone I called thought I was in a quiet room at home and could clearly hear me, not the chaos around me.

Thankfully, everything else about these earbuds is solid too. The mini-stabilizers on the top end of the buds help keep them secure, so they stayed steady while working out. IP55 water and dust resistance and 6.5 hours of battery life (28 with the case) make them very versatile. And active noise-canceling (ANC) far exceeds my expectations. While it’s not quite as good as Apple’s and Bose’s flagship buds, it’s close, and for a lot less money.

The only nitpicks I notice are that they sound a bit bass-heavy out of the box (you can adjust this in the app, however), and they are a little big. That’s not much criticism for such a solid pair of earbuds.

There’s a reason everyone (myself included) recommends Apple AirPods Pro 3. They aren’t just the “default” option. They are incredibly good wireless earbuds for anyone with an iPhone. They offer the most seamless, fully featured earbud experience you can get on iOS, with instant pairing out of the box. They sound clear and detailed, whether you are listening to music or on a call with friends. And noise-canceling and transparency are some of the best on the market. AirPods can work with non-Apple devices, but you lose access to many features, like Siri voice assistance.

This latest version uses a new foam-lined ear tip that took a little getting used to but delivered significantly improved noise isolation, even before turning on noise-canceling. Battery life is also improved (up to eight hours per charge), as is water and dust resistance (an above-average IP57). These earbuds also have surprisingly accurate built-in heart rate sensors, so you can track your workouts without a fitness tracker or smartwatch. Plus, these earbuds support a bevy of Apple software features, including real-time translation.

The Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro are the best earbuds for anyone who already owns and uses a Samsung phone or Samsung smartwatch, similar to AirPods for Apple users. That comparison isn’t just surface level: These are the most AirPods-like Samsung earbuds yet; the size, shape, fit, and feel are very AirPods Pro 3.

These are fun, comfortable, and convenient earbuds for anyone with a Samsung phone. The noise-canceling works admirably, canceling out most low drones like plane and AC noise and reducing café and office chatter. Ambient Sound (aka transparency mode) is a real standout—it’s clear and natural-sounding, so much so that we used it instead of open earbuds for walks and hikes on occasion. Paired with a Samsung phone, there are features galore: a customizable nine-band equalizer (with presets), earbud fit tests, high-resolution audio support, voice control settings (Google Assistant or Bixby), Find My Earbuds (think Apple Find My), and more. But, importantly, they sound great straight out of the box.

The only downside is battery life: Six hours of playback with ANC puts it behind most other earbuds on this list. And controls, while simple and intuitive, misfired semi-often over several days of testing.

If you’re on Android and want something a little smaller and lighter than the Liberty 5 Pro, consider Google’s Pixel Buds Pro 2. They are small, lightweight, and very comfortable, with all the flagship performance you would expect: great noise-canceling and transparency, detailed sound quality, and superb battery life. Like the Liberty 5 Pro, they have a mini wing-tip that fits in your ear and helps keep these buds stable during more intense workouts. But unlike those buds, these are much smaller and a bit more comfortable to wear all day. Being Google buds, you can, unsurprisingly, prompt Gemini straight from the buds to answer questions or act as a voice assistant.

Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen) Specs

Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen) will truly quiet the world around you. While many earbuds on this list come close, none match the ANC on these earbuds. They are the benchmark I compare other earbuds against. Airplanes, subways, cars, cafes—nearly all noise gets dialed down.

Thankfully, they sound great too, with detailed bass, mids, and treble, plus a few spatial audio features to experiment with. Aside from the above-average price, the main con is that these buds are big. Like, really big. I’m used to it now, but my friends have pointed out, multiple times, how big these things are.

JLab is my go-to brand for budget earbuds, and the Go Pop ANC are a prime example of why. These buds are shockingly full-featured for $30: ANC and transparency modes that actually work, stable Bluetooth connectivity, a robust app with adjustable EQ and programmable controls, and a respectable IP55 dust- and water-resistance rating. I can think of many earbuds over $100 that mess up the basics more than these ones do. Sure, I found the tiny USB-C cable more annoying than helpful (it's short and built into the case), but at this price, it’s hard to nitpick.

Open earbuds rest on or wrap around the outside of your ears, leaving them open to hear the world around you. They’re an excellent choice when you want to be aware of your surroundings—think walking, running, biking, or hiking outdoors.

After testing dozens, I almost always come back to Shokz OpenDots. They have been my constant, consistent companion for walks, runs, bike rides, and just living life. For me, the combination of comfort, ease of use, and battery life puts them ahead of competitors. I’ve worn these earbuds for hours at a time and completely forgotten I was wearing them. Which is especially easy to do because the buds get up to 10 hours of battery life, way more than most of my recommendations on this list.

Open earbuds as a whole don’t sound nearly as good as in-ear earbuds, but the OpenDots 2 do a fine job of conveying detailed instrumentation in such a small form factor.

The controls have been consistent and responsive in my testing, though part of me wishes Shokz opted for real buttons (like the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds) instead of touch-sensitive areas around the barrel/battery cell.

If you’re really locked in on open-ear headphones for fitness, the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are the better buy, but OpenDots win on versatility and convenience.

The Beats PowerBeats Pro 2 are capital-W workout earbuds. Part of the reason is fit—these earbuds stay in my ears no matter what kind of workouts I do. I once tried to make them fall out by smacking my ears with my hands for a good five seconds. They didn’t budge.

They are massively improved from the 2019 originals. The earbuds are much smaller and comfier; they have solid noise canceling and transparency modes, plus built-in heart rate sensors, so you can record heart rate data without a smartwatch or fitness tracker. They’re also great on both iPhones and Android phones: Apple’s H2 chip adds Find My support, Siri voice assistant, and iCloud device switching, while Android users get a dedicated Beats app and easy one-touch pairing.

My main gripe with them is that they are only IPX4 dust- and water-resistant, which is particularly baffling for workout headphones (even the all-purpose AirPods Pro 3 are IP57). They’re also still a bit big, but that’s necessary for such a secure ear-hook design. If you want a more streamlined workout earbud, I also love the smaller Beats Powerbeats Fit, though they don’t have a built-in heart rate sensor.

I test new earbuds every month. These models made an impression but didn’t quite make it into my top picks.

Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging Case for $149: If you are dead set on Apple earbuds, but don’t love the feeling of silicone in your ear, Apple AirPods 5 are your best bet. They have a semi-open-ear fit (no eartips!) that doesn’t block out noise like AirPods Pro 3 do. And the ANC, while not as good as the Pro 3’s, is excellent for an open-ear design and a huge improvement over AirPods 4. Still, I prefer AirPods Pro 3 for most occasions, and they do go on sale often, if price is a deciding factor.

Sony WH-1000XM6 for $330: If you want premium design and excellent sound quality, these latest flagship earbuds from Sony fit the bill. With excellent ANC and transparency modes, plus a truly detailed sound profile, they scored a 9/10 in our Sony WH-1000XM6 review. What kept them out of the top spot is fit and price. I couldn’t find the right foam earbud to fit comfortably in my ear, no matter what sizes I used. (This rarely, if ever, happens when I test earbuds.) They’re also $330—that’s a high price, especially when so many competitors offer a similarly great experience for less.

Nothing Ear (3a) for $99: These stylish little earbuds stand out from the crowd with a bold design and a sub-$100 price. Even at this price, they don’t really leave anything out. They pair easily with iPhone and Android devices; have a fully fledged app with features like a customizable EQ, call recording, and audio transcriptions; and sound great. ANC could be better, but again, at this price, it’s hard to complain. You can learn more in our Nothing Ear (3a) review.

Soundcore Liberty 5 for $130: I prefer stem-shaped earbuds, and these from Soundcore are excellent for the price, though they’re a bit outgunned by the Liberty 5 Pro. They fit comfortably and deliver above-average sound quality and noise-canceling. But they don’t have the outstanding call quality of the Pro version (it’s still good, just not as good). Their saving grace compared to their bigger brother is size—these are much smaller, lighter earbuds you may find more comfortable.

Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 for $180: The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are some of my favorite headphones for running and cycling. They are open-ear headphones that let you easily hear the world around you, great for staying aware while exercising outdoors. Nowadays, I tend to prefer the smaller size of open earbuds like the Shokz OpenDots 2. But the larger size of these headphones means better bass, clearer sound, and longer battery life than smaller open earbuds.

Soundcore Space A40 for $80: The Soundcore Space A40 used to be some of my favorite earbuds for the price. That is, before the Nothing Ear (3a) and Soundcore’s own Liberty 5 and Liberty 5 Pro came along. They still offer some great sound and noise-canceling for the price, and if you prefer a pebble-style form factor, these may be just right for you.

Google Pixel Buds 2a for $129: The Pixel Buds 2a are a former top pick (replaced by the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro) and are still a great budget option, especially for anyone who wants something small and light. They share a lot with the pricier Pixel Buds Pro 2, including a comfortable fit, built-in stabilizer, great battery life, and instant pairing with Android phones. They don’t support wireless charging, however.

Sony Linkbuds Fit for $230: I wanted to like the Sony Linkbuds Fit more than I did. They are very comfortable, with a super soft built-in stabilizer that keeps the earbuds feeling stable even during workouts and runs. The issue is the touch controls: they aren’t very responsive. I often had to press commands multiple times for the Linkbuds to register what I was doing, and sometimes they wouldn’t respond at all. Plus, at $230, the competition is simply superior.

Beats Solo Buds for $80: The Beats Solo Buds are small, lightweight, and have great battery life on a single charge. But that’s where the compliments end. The earbuds don’t have noise-canceling or transparency of any kind. And the tiny earbud case doesn’t provide any extra charge. Buy the Soundcore Space A40 instead, or spend a little more to get the Nothing Ear (3a) or Soundcore Liberty 5.

Samsung Galaxy Buds4 for $180: I didn’t find these earbuds very comfortable to wear, and the noise-canceling is not very effective compared to a traditional ear tip design or the new Apple AirPods 5. But the main issue here is price. You can get so many better earbuds for $180, including the often-on-sale Samsung Galaxy Buds Pro 3.

I test wireless earbuds in the real world, not in a testing lab. I wear them in my daily life, which means hanging out at home, commuting on the train, working in the office, going to the gym, running (and cycling) outdoors, flying coach, you name it.

Noise cancellation, call quality, and sound quality are three things I test particularly hard. The New York City subway and downtown, plus my office building’s cafeteria, are great places to push noise-canceling to its limits. Same with call quality (though I also test this using my office's phone booths as a consistent control).

Sound quality is a bit more subjective, but I do have a few favorite playlists and songs I listen to with every earbud I test. My main audio source is Spotify Lossless, and, when possible, I test multiple audio codecs.

#339. Razer unveils the Raiju V3 Pro Signature Edition PS5 controller

It sure is pretty and will likely be expensive.

Razer just announced the Razer Raiju V3 Pro Signature Edition controller, a flagship gamepad made specifically for PS5 consoles. It looks absolutely gorgeous, with an open-shell design you can see into. See-through stuff is all the rage right now. There's also a big PlayStation button and a Razer logo up top.

It was built with premium materials. The black exoskeleton is made from magnesium alloy and there's a nano coating over the internals to keep out debris. Even the touchpad is semi-transparent, which is manufactured with laser-etched glass. The whole thing weighs just 260 grams, which is lighter than a standard DualSense controller. That's pretty cool.

Now let's move on to features. This is a pro-grade controller, so it can do a lot. It includes contactless TMR thumbsticks which should help with aiming precision. There are six mappable buttons, including two claw-grip bumpers and four mouse-click back buttons. These can be used to map hotkeys and the like. The buttons are made from durable polybutylene terephthalate, also called PBT. This is an extremely rigid and durable plastic.

It can be used with other devices, even though it has a big PlayStation logo. It looks especially useful for PC gamers, as it offers up to a 2,000Hz HyperPolling wireless rate. This means that it sends data to and from the PC 2,000 times every second.

The controller arrives in a collector's edition that includes a bunch of extra goodies. The package ships with a leatherette carrying case, alternate thumbstick caps, back button covers, a wireless dongle and tools for replacing parts.

The Razer Raiju V3 Pro Signature Edition will be available on November 10, but potential buyers had better not dilly-dally. The company says it's only making 1,337 of these things. That number might elicit a chuckle from some and a groan from others, as this is an old-school example of "leetspeak."

Razer hasn't released a price, but chances are it'll probably cost a pretty penny.

#337. I Tried Amazon’s New Kindles. Buy This Accessory Instead (2026)

Amazon’s Kindle e-readers have a whole new look this fall. There are three new Kindle models, gorgeous metallic colors, and several new accessories. The beauty of the metallic options has caught the eye of most of my friends (and even my editor, who is not usually a fan of e-readers), but if there’s one thing you should buy out of all the new Kindle gear, it's the least expensive offering: the Amazon Kindle Click ($35).

The Kindle Click is Amazon's first Bluetooth Kindle page turner that will pair with its two latest generations of Kindles, from both 2024 and 2026. Many of us have been using third-party page-turning remotes for our Kindles for a while, but these designs are often cumbersome, with screen-blocking clips and multiple components to keep track of. Now there’s a single device that costs a little more than some of the third-party designs but works much better. It’s the Kindle accessory I’m recommending everyone buy (so long as you have a compatible Kindle, of course).

The Kindle Click is a lightweight handheld remote that connects to your Kindle e-reader over Bluetooth, letting you turn pages, scroll up and down your screen, and even adjust the brightness. Two large buttons on the front turn the page, and then two smaller buttons on the right ridge let you adjust the brightness. The brightness adjustment was more useful to me than I expected, and a really nice bonus for such an inexpensive accessory. It charges via USB-C and comes with a little wrist strap, so if you were to let go of it, you won’t drop it.

The only slightly unintuitive thing is that when you use the buttons to click down a page, the higher button moves you down the page while the lower button moves you back up. It makes sense once you think about it, but it might throw you off at first from a visual perspective until you get the hang of it.

A Kindle page turner is a nice accessibility accessory for folks who might not be able to comfortably hold up their Kindle and tap the pages regularly. I love it as a gal who has struggled with wrist cysts, and plenty of my fellow Kindle users have setups where a remote would come in handy just for their own comfort. Obviously, if the Kindle is sitting in your hand, you probably don’t want the remote in your hand at the same time, so I think this is best paired with some kind of Kindle holder or repurposed tablet holder. I have a few favorites, but there are tons of options out there.

The Click’s design is a huge improvement over the typical aftermarket options. I found those models irritating because they usually had two separate parts—a clip you attach to your screen, which often blocked part of it, and a separate remote that you hold. Both of them needed to be charged separately. Now, I’m free of that burden and free of charging tiny batteries that only seemed to last one reading session. The Kindle Click doesn't specify battery life beyond “lasts for weeks,” but with how much larger the Click body is compared to cheap third-party options, I'm hopeful the battery itself is bigger.

Kindle Click from the front, with the main buttons.

Kindle Click from the side, with the brightness buttons.

The Click is nearly half the price of the new Kindle page-turn cover ($80) that I also really like, but you also need one of the new Kindle Signature Editions to use. Those models start at $250, so if you’re buying a new e-reader specifically for physical page-turn buttons, you end up spending $330; at that point, I would say go buy a Kobo Libra Colour ($258), which has built-in page-turn buttons, instead and save yourself around $75. (More if you compare it to the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition with this button case—you'd spend a full $400 to get both of those.) I do really like the case; it's just too expensive and comes with the roadblock of needing the newest, most expensive model to access it.

Meanwhile, the Kindle Click works with any Kindle from 2024 onward, though there are plenty of Kindle readers who don’t have such a recent model, so you might still need to upgrade. (If that’s the case, I would keep an eye out for what’s going to go on sale for Black Friday. I don’t have huge hopes that the newest models will be on sale yet, but the 2024 model should be and is still a great Kindle, even if it’s not the newest one.)

Whether you're shopping for yourself or a gift for a book lover this holiday season, I think this gadget is truly both affordable and useful. It's already taking a few weeks to ship after launching last week, so if you want this handy remote before the holidays, start shopping sooner rather than later.

#336. Why large dogs age faster than small ones, and other October research highlights

Plus invisible tattoos, medieval skeleton gets an ID, trapping a single antimatter particle, and more.

It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. October’s list includes an epigenetic mechanism for why large dogs age faster than smaller ones; physicists who trapped a single particle of antimatter for months; and invisible tattoo inks that only show up under UV light.

In many mammalian species, larger creatures tend to have longer lifespans. Mice, for instance, live an average of just two years, while some whales can last for as long as 200 years. Dogs, however, buck this pattern; larger dogs tend to age faster and die younger than smaller ones, which makes canines an ideal model for biologists to study to learn more about aging in general. Arizona State University scientists report that these lifespan differences seem to be due to so-called “jumping genes,” according to a paper published in the journal Science.

The authors used data from 864 dogs collected in the Dog Aging Project to map patterns of DNA methylation (which influences how much certain genes are turned on or off) across the entire genome. It’s part of the epigenome, whose markers can change over time in response to stress and other environmental factors. Genetic sequences, by contrast, are largely fixed. So DNA methylation is a good chemical indicator of aging and DNA regulation.

Their analysis showed that aging in dogs is linked to the decrease in the regulation provided by DNA methylation, particularly in regions where there are “jumping genes” that can move from chromosome to chromosome. These jumps can damage DNA, causing cancer and other age-related diseases, and their activity increases with the loss of regulatory markers. The authors identified a specific class of jumping genes called LINE1s that were responsible for the different rates of aging in dogs. Giant dog breeds lost roughly 35 percent more LINE1 methylation each year compared to small breeds.

“This is one of the clearest molecular signatures we’ve seen that aligns with the well-known size-lifespan trade-off in dogs,” said co-author Blaise Mariner. “It suggests that faster aging in larger dogs may be driven, at least in part, by reduced control over these jumping genes.”

Science, 2026. DOI: 10.1126/science.aeb2986 (About DOIs).

One of the biggest unanswered questions in cosmology is why the early Universe had a fundamental asymmetry between matter and antimatter. When matter and antimatter particles collide, they annihilate into energy, so that asymmetry resulted in matter dominating our Universe, which contains much more matter than antimatter. It’s extremely difficult to create and isolate antimatter, requiring special traps. Physicists at Northwestern University have succeeded in trapping a single positron (antimatter particle) for months on end, according to a paper published in Physical Review Letters.

Co-author Gerald Gabrielse and his team built on earlier work, in which they trapped a single electron to create a one-electron quantum cyclotron. They then used the setup to make one of the most precise measurements of its magnetic moment yet. Trapping a positron was a bit trickier. They harvested the positron from sodium-22 nuclei, slowing it down enough to guide it into a near-perfect vacuum trap of electric and magnetic fields. Once inside, they chilled the positron to just 300 millikelvins (0.3° above absolute zero), thereby keeping the positron in its quantum ground state. They found they could maintain that state for months at a time.

That enabled Gabrielse et al. to manipulate and detect the particle’s individual quantum energy state using tuned microwaves—the first critical step in being able to measure the positron’s magnetic properties, hopefully with the same precision they achieved in their earlier experiments with a single electron. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that there should be no difference between the two particle measurements. If they are not equal, “that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century,” said Gabrielse.

Physical Review Letters, 2026. DOI: 10.1103/gbkc-6nlj.

Credit: Matter & Light, Bruns et al./CC BY-SA Credit: Matter & Light, Bruns et al./CC BY-SA

Many people sport tattoos, but there are situations where hiding them is desirable. A new line of multicolored tattoo inks could one day make that dilemma moot; they are invisible to the human eye unless one illuminates them with UV light, according to a paper published in the journal Matter & Light. “There’s a stigma, in science and in many cultures, around body art,” said co-author Carson Bruns of the University of Colorado, Boulder, who sports a green lion tattoo on one arm, among others. “I’m proud to be pushing against that.”

As previously reported, epidermal electronics attached to the skin via temporary tattoos (e-tattoos) have been around for more than a decade. So-called e-tattoos connect to skin without adhesives, are practically unnoticeable, and are typically attached via temporary tattoo, allowing electrical measurements (and other measurements, such as temperature and strain) using ultra-thin polymers with embedded circuit elements. In 2024, researchers developed special polymer-based conductive inks that can be printed onto a person’s scalp to measure brain waves, even if they have hair. This could one day enable mobile EEG monitoring outside a clinical setting, among other potential applications. And earlier this year, scientists at Pennsylvania State University developed a novel conductive ink that can be painted directly onto the skin in colorful custom designs, turning into a functional electrode for biomonitoring after drying.

Bruns et al. created their inks, known as PhotoTat, from color-changing dyes injected into tiny spheres of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), a material used in dermal fillers among other medical applications. Mixing the primary-colored dyes can create full-color images. The tattoos are invisible until exposed to UV light, when they turn blue, magenta, or yellow. They fade after a few hours, faster if exposed to bright LED light. It’s still a proof of concept, but Bruns did test the dyes on himself, inking a black outline of fish scales that turn red, orange, or blue, like mermaid scales, under UV light. The dyes could also help cancer patients undergoing radiation therapy, who need small tattoos so doctors can guide the beams. PhotoTat would make such tattoos invisible except when the treatment is being administered.

Matter & Light, 2026. 10.1016/j.matlit.2026.100119.

Credit: Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd./CC BY-ND Credit: Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd./CC BY-ND

Over 150 years ago, archaeologists discovered a skeleton buried in a Roman sarcophagus on the grounds of Westminster Abbey, bearing an inscription to a wealthy Briton from between 300 to 400 CE named Valerius Amandinus. But there was also a Latin cross sculpted into the lid that dated to the 10th or 11th century, i.e., the late Saxon period. Were the remains actually those of someone who lived and died centuries after Valerius? According to a paper published in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association, they are—specifically, these are the bones of a high-ranking medieval monk.

The authors reasoned that this was an abbot’s skeleton because it was buried within a sarcophagus, while skeletal clues suggested it was a man between 35 and 49, standing about 5 feet, 9 inches tall. The most likely conclusion is that the bones belong to a Benedictine monk named Aelfwig, who died around 1020 and was buried at Westminster Abbey, where he had served as abbot. However, the bones may also be those of Aelfwig’s successor, Wulboth, who died in 1049 and was likely buried on the grounds as well. There is also evidence that the body was originally housed in a timber coffin that decayed over the ensuing seven centuries.

Journal of the British Archaeological Association, 2026. DOI: 10.1080/00681288.2026.2675788.

Credit: Sandro Botticelli/Public domain Credit: Sandro Botticelli/Public domain

In June, we reported on the research of Paolo Pozzilli of Queen Mary University of London and several co-authors into the cause of death of one of Sandro Botticelli’s models. Among his best-known works is the Birth of Venus, depicting the naked goddess, newly birthed, standing in a giant scallop shell. The model for the painting (disputed by some historians) was allegedly Simonetta Vespucci (née Cattaneo), a renowned beauty in Florentine high society whom Botticelli greatly admired. He painted her five times before her untimely death in her early 20s.

It was long believed that Simonetta had succumbed to tuberculosis, but it was argued that she may have suffered from a pituitary tumor (adenoma) that gradually increased in size due to prolactin and growth hormone secretions, citing her appearance in several portraits as evidence. This could have caused a sudden tumor-related fatal apoplexy. They examined letters between Simonetta’s father-in-law, Piero Vespucci, and Lorenzo de Medici, which described how Simonetta had collapsed during a ball a few days before her death. Her symptoms included headache, hallucinations, vomiting, and a high fever, all symptoms of a rapidly expanding pituitary tumor, per the authors.

Pozzilli et al. are back again with a paper published in the journal Medical Humanities providing further evidence for their hypothesis about Vespucci’s cause of death. They argued that the tumor could also explain the irregular eye positioning in the Birth of Venus, suggesting the model had a squint or eye misalignment. After more closely studying how Botticelli depicted the model’s eyes in Birth of Venus and several other portraits, the authors noted pronounced swelling around the left eye, likely due to fluid buildup, while some of the tissue covering the white part of the eye is loose. This and the telltale squint support the theory that Simonetta had a tumor in her pituitary gland.

Medical Humanities, 2026. DOI: 10.1136/medhum-2026-014199.

Credit: Public domain Credit: Public domain

Vincent van Gogh’s masterpiece, The Starry Night (1889), has long fascinated art lovers and scientists like. Some physicists have even suggested that the painting is a masterful depiction of atmospheric turbulence, and a 2024 paper found that the illusion of movement in the blue sky is also due to the scale of the paint strokes—a second kind of “hidden turbulence” at the microscale that diffuses throughout the entire canvas, although others have objected to that conclusion. Now a team of South Korean astronomers has used “forensic astronomy” to pinpoint the precise month in which van Gogh painted his masterpiece, according to a paper published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Other astronomers have previously suggested that The Starry Night is not just a symbolic representation, but shows the actual night sky at the time it was created, specifically in June 1889. This new analysis—which takes into account simulations, historical weather patterns, star positions, and van Gogh’s letters from that year—shifts that date to just before dawn on July 22, 1889. Co-author Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim told Gizmodo that his interest was piqued when he came across previous research identifying the constellation Aries. Kim thought the lights in the painting more closely resembled the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus, suggesting the July date. While van Gogh said that his work exaggerated the point of view he painted, the authors note that such exaggeration “presupposes a real object to amplify.”

Kim et al. are in good company in forensic astronomy. As we reported in 2020, the so-called “celestial sleuth,” Donald Olson, applied similar tools to determine that Vermeer’s View of Delft most likely shows the city on September 3 or 4, 1659 (or earlier), at 8 am. Over the years, Olson has found evidence that the blood-red sunset that inspired Edvard Munch’s The Scream was likely an aftereffect of the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa in Indonesia; that the Moon may have contributed to the sinking of the Titanic; helped identify the precise location of Julius Caesar’s landing site in Britain in 55 BC; and showed that Mary Shelley was probably telling the truth about a moonlit “waking dream” that inspired Frankenstein. And in 2015, Olson determined the precise time of day that Life magazine photographer Alfred Eisenstaedt took his most famous photograph (V-J- Day in Times Square) on August 14, 1945.

Scientific Reports, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-73025-5.

With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#334. How to use your phone to find hidden cameras

When you feel wary, a quick check might provide some peace of mind.

For those of us who travel often, staying in a new location carries an unsettling risk: Airbnbs, hotels and other lodgings may have hidden cameras to spy on visitors. Short-term and privately owned rentals are of particular concern. While the full scale of the issue is unknown, a 2024 report from CNN found that Airbnb processed 35,000 support tickets related to "surveillance devices" in the preceding decade. While doorbell and outdoor security cameras have become increasingly common and are permitted under Airbnb rules, any indoor recording devices are banned from properties hosted on the platform.

The problem remains relatively uncommon. Airbnb said at the time of the CNN report that less than 0.1 percent of its properties were hit with safety complaints, including those related to security cameras. However, 51 percent of visitors said they don't trust short-term rentals, and such fears are not unfounded. Cameras are increasingly difficult to spot, often disguised as common home items like smoke detectors, chargers or picture frames. So it can sometimes be worth a check to ensure there are no surveillance devices in your lodging to ease your mind. But how do you find hidden cameras?

Your cell phone is a great tool to check for hidden cameras. Start with a simple flashlight sweep: close the curtains, turn off the lights, and then sweep the unit with a flashlight to check for any glimmering signs of electronics — the shine of a lens, or an LED light. Common places to hide cameras include smoke detectors, air purifiers, televisions, shower heads, or lights. Be particularly careful to check sensitive locations like near the bed or the shower. Mirrors are also important to check. If you shine a flashlight at a mirror, it should bounce back rather than passing through like a window. You can also put a finger directly onto a mirror. A real mirror will have a space between your finger and its reflection, while a two-way mirror will make it appear as though they are directly touching.

You can also use your phone camera to check for night-vision cameras in the room. These cameras emit infrared light, which on your camera app should appear as purple or white dots. To verify your phone can detect infrared light, point it at a TV remote control, push the buttons, and see if light coming from the remote can be detected. It is more likely your front-facing, or selfie camera, has this ability, but try using both to take a look. Once confirmed, you can scan the room with your phone to find IR emissions.

Many hidden cameras stream over Wi-Fi, and some mobile apps allow you to scan the network for unfamiliar devices. Options include Fing, Net Analyzer and WiFiman. Download a scanner app, connect to the Wi-Fi and search for names that you don't recognize — which will often include "cam" or "camera" to denote a recording device. Other names may map to common camera brands, like Wyze, Blink or TP-Link. Apps like Fing will show MAC addresses and device types, allowing you to further investigate names that show up in a scan. This is not always a straightforward method, however. Some devices like printers, televisions or other benign connected appliances are also likely to show up in such scans.

What's more, other devices may run their own networks, so check your phone's list of available Wi-Fi networks for similar, camera-related titles. Other cameras may use Bluetooth to connect, so a Bluetooth scan may also be helpful. To do this, you don't necessarily need a scanner app. You can just open your Bluetooth connections on the device and see what shows up.

These methods are not foolproof. Many cameras record to local memory cards, which means they won't show up on any kind of scan. Still, pairing this method with the flashlight sweep and the infrared light check is the most thorough way to check for surveillance.

If you think you have found a surveillance device in your lodging, be sure to double check using both the physical sweep method and digital scan. Once you have confirmed, do not touch the device: photograph it, reach out to the police and notify customer support for the platform you are using. Airbnb has clear policies against indoor cameras, even those that are not connected, and has in several reported cases removed hosts from the platform permanently and fully refunded guests who report such devices.

Vrbo also bans recording devices outright, and suggests guests who discover one report the incident immediately to the platform. Vrbo's policy states affected guests may be eligible for a refund. The CNN report regarding hidden cameras at Airbnb found there is no strict policy guiding employees to contact law enforcement in such incidents, so it's best to contact police yourself if you feel unsafe. Ultimately, a scan with your phone's flashlight, an infrared check with a camera and a sweep with a dedicated app can give you increased peace of mind when staying in an unfamiliar location.

#333. Asian Cup postponed due to Middle East conflict

The Asian Cup has become the latest sporting event to be affected by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Organizers cite "exceptional circumstances" in Saudi Arabia, which has seen several Houthi attacks of late.

A little over two months before it was set to kick off, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has postponed its flagship international football tournament in the wake of recent deadly attacks on host country, Saudi Arabia.

The AFC cited "substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions" caused by conflicts in the region.

Instead of January 7, 2027, the tournament will now kick off on December 23 and end on January 21, 2028. The postponement follows delays and cancellations of a number of sporting events in the region, including a Formula One race, the men's and women's tennis finals, the 2027 Dakar Rally and disruption to Asia's marquee continental club football tournament, the AFC Champions League Elite.

Saudi Arabia hosted, and won, the Gulf Cup last month, but there had already been much talk about whether the much larger Asian Cup could go ahead.

It was scheduled to feature 24 teams playing matches in eight venues across Riyadh, Jeddah and Khobar. However, the AFC said that "circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions," made the tournament impossible.

"Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organization and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders."

In particular, the postponement was forced by a recent wave of deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi rebels as well as other raging conflicts in the region. The Houthis have targeted Saudi infrastructure, including airports. They are fighting a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government, a civil war that reignited in July following a years-long truce.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The AFC had been under pressure from several federations to postpone the tournament, with South Korea's players leading the way.

"The ongoing military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that cannot be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, president of the Korea Professional Footballers Association, said last month, according to the Yonhap News Agency.

Lee added that "no tournament's value can take precedence over the lives and safety of players and football fans."

It seems that the AFC now agrees. However, following the announcement of the postponement, Yasser al-Misehal, chairman of the local organizing committee, promised that Saudi Arabia was "fully ready" whenever the tournament ended up being held.

"The tournament will move to the new dates, and our preparations will continue as planned," he told the Saudi Press Agency.

"We're working closely with the AFC and all our partners to make sure the tournament runs smoothly and meets the high standards expected of Saudi Arabia and the Asian Cup."

Saudi Arabia has invested hugely in sports over the last decade, from owning Premier League teams to hosting boxing title fights and bidding for a number of major sporting events, most notably World Cup 2034, which they won the right to host unopposed.

However, the country has recently withdrawn or slashed funding for a number of sporting events including golf, rugby, tennis and winter sports.

#331. eharmony app reviews: Subscribers share whether it’s worth it

It's incredible that eharmony has managed to stay relevant in the online dating world. The dating site launched back at the turn of the millennium and held firm by focusing on a more substantive, personality-based approach to online matchmaking. It's not perfect, of course, and different daters prefer different approaches to finding partners.

While eharmony members generally appreciate the depth of its matchmaking algorithm, they sometimes complain about the cost and the number of fake profiles, particularly since artificial intelligence has become more widely available.

Here's what real eharmony users had to say about the site, from the best features to the worst experiences:

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups

Pure — best for anonymous hookups

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

If you're looking for some genuine substance on dating sites, you often have to filter out all the people who are only in it for short-term fun. At least, that's the case on other dating platforms. But eharmony largely bypasses that problem, first through its reputation (fun fact: it began as a Christian dating site!) and through its detailed sign-up process, which includes completing the eharmony compatibility questionnaire.

Reddit reviewers have consistently lauded this focus on substance in the screening process ("it forces you to focus on depth over pure visuals") and found the compatibility scores, assigned based on your answers to the personality quiz you take when you sign up, to be a useful way of evaluating matches before starting a conversation.

Here's a story from one older gentleman: "My mindset was that I really needed to be fully honest in my answers, because why would I pay for a service and not be honest? After a few days, I got my matches. A day later, I got a nice message from a woman 10 years younger than me. We exchanged some messages, and then I looked at our match score after she prompted me about it. We were 126 out of 140. I decided to go with it because she and I were really vibing on each other. A year later we got engaged and will marry next year."

For reference, a compatibility score of 126 on eharmony is incredibly rare. As one Redditor responded, "When I was on there, I never had greater than 105 with any match."

A common complaint over the years about eharmony has been the cost of the premium membership, which you need to sign up for to get the most out of the site (eharmony doesn't even let you see photos without upgrading to its premium service). There are three premium membership tiers to choose from (Light, Plus, and Unlimited), with pricing varying somewhat by your location, but you should expect to pay at least $15 per month for a membership, which makes it more expensive than a standard Netflix subscription but around the same price as a cheap gym membership.

Users have complained about both the price and the cancellation process: "I’ve tried eHarmony and found it way too expensive for what it offers, and to top it [off], the process of cancellation is so complicated," said one Reddit reviewer. Other users were unhappy with its automatic membership renewals or the difficulty of canceling a subscription, even just 12 hours after signing up.

That said, eharmony entices users with steep discounts — sometimes up to 50 percent off the regular membership price — so if you keep tabs on offers, you can sign up and get substantial savings.

It's a fact of online dating: different sites are built for different demographics. That means certain age groups gravitate towards certain sites. You'll already know that if you've ever used Tinder as a middle-aged adult.

Older daters, divorced daters, and anyone looking for a more mature partner should definitely try eharmony. We named it the "gold standard" for daters over 40 for a reason — the older age bracket is eharmony's wheelhouse.

Here's a typical experience from an older male dater: "45 yo divorced guy here. I signed up with eHarmony and Bumble 2 months ago based on recommendations from co-workers. I've had much better luck with eHarmony than Bumble. My highest compatibility ratings are in the 110 to 116 range, and these comprise about 33 percent of my daily feed. The other 33 percent are in the 100 to 105 rating scale, and the final 33 percent are in the 89 to 99 rating scale. [...] In contrast, I have connected with zero women on Bumble Premium after 2 months."

In the age of AI and cheaply produced deepfakes, dating sites have been swamped by fake profiles. Indeed, eharmony users have found themselves sifting through numerous fake dating profiles before finding a real human being to engage. It's frustrating.

One of the top-rated posts on the /r/eharmony subreddit in the last year decries, "The fake profile problem has got noticeably worse," complaining that of the 14 likes their account received, 11 came from obviously fake accounts.

But how big a problem is this, really? For older daters unaccustomed to filtering out fake profiles and photos, it can be a major pain in the butt, sure. But if you're even remotely internet-savvy, you shouldn't have too much trouble distinguishing between real and fake users. And you're guarantee you'll encounter this problem on pretty much every dating platform — so don't let it put you off using eharmony. And because eharmony has tight restrictions for free members, you can largely side-step the fake profile issue if you upgrade to a paid subscription. This allows you to only interact with other paying members, which effectively eliminates those annoying bots.

#330. ‘I’m 100 Percent at War with Trump’: MAGA Revolts After Midterms Wipeout

Many MAGAworld figures are already pointing the finger of blame for their midterm losses squarely at president Donald Trump and his policies.

Trump spent Tuesday evening lashing out at Fox News for platforming the Democrats who swept aside their GOP opponents in deep red states and took control of the House and Senate.

“[Fox] bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse,” the president wrote on Truth Social. Later in the night, he called in to Fox News, where he congratulated the Democrats on their results.

Trump made clear that he doesn’t think the historic blowout was a reflection of his popularity, writing “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” He then posted a picture of a red baseball hat with the word VETO embossed on the front.

But in the hours that followed, MAGA revolted.

Matt Walsh, a right-wing podcaster, called the results “a political catastrophe of historic proportions” and Trump “a 80 year old lame duck president.” Walsh blamed Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran and his focus on trivial matters like attempting to rename artificial intelligence super intelligence and the White House ballroom.

For right-wing commentator Mike Cernovich, it was Trump’s decision to ostracize libertarian voters that was partly to blame.

Mike Flynn, the disgraced former national security adviser who was among the most prominent voices pushing bogus conspiracies about the 2020 election being stolen, also blamed Trump, writing on X that “Someone needs to look in a mirror.” Flynn also blamed Christians for not showing up to vote.

But noted conspiracy theorist Alex Jones had another take on why Trump was to blame.

“I think he’s a Democrat, I’m gonna just say it right now,” Jones said on his show Tuesday night. “I’ve tried to salvage Trump, I’ve not been sure, I’ve invested so much—maybe I was blind to it—I think he’s the ultimate Democrat sleeper cell and he works for them. I’m 100 percent at war with Trump.”

Other MAGA figures like right-wing commentators Jack Posobiec and Nick Sortor both blamed Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran for the losses, but didn’t directly name Trump in their posts.

Unsurprisingly, Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former congresswoman who broke decisively with Trump earlier this year, also blamed the president. “Tonight was a total referendum on Trump. He told people to vote like he was on the ballot and they did,” Greene wrote on X.

One notable aspect of MAGAworld’s response to Tuesday’s GOP wipeout was the relative silence coming from some of Trump’s biggest supporters.

Elon Musk, who poured hundreds of millions of dollars into supporting losing Republican candidates, has not said who was to blame for the results. He did post a joke saying his ”election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time” and commented that it was “interesting” that an exit poll showed the Iran war was a “massive losing issue.”

Rogan O’Handley, a vocal MAGA influencer known as DC Draino who posts incessantly on X about politics, has also not reacted publicly to the results. Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, who was reelected on Tuesday night, said the results were “not what we’d hoped and fought for,” but failed to say what or who was to blame.

White House deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser Stephen Miller has also not commented publicly on the results, but his wife, Katie Miller, who boosted election conspiracy theories earlier on Tuesday, laid the blame on the media, which she called “a propaganda arm of the woke left.”

There were, however, a few right-wing figures who continued to publicly support Trump despite the losses, including MAGA influencer Laura Loomer, who wrote, “President Trump is a hero for stopping Iran from having a nuclear weapon, and now he should finish the job.” Instead of blaming Trump, Loomer spent Tuesday evening lamenting the end of America and the rise of communism.

Another right-wing figure continuing to back Trump was the former Fox News host-turned-conspiracy theorist Lara Logan, who blamed an anonymous group of Republicans who conspired to bring about the defeat so they could “get rid of the MAGA movement and the establishment would retake the party.”

Chaya Raichik, who runs the hugely popular LibsofTikTok accounts, blamed the losses on a years-long Democrat plot to import “millions of foreigners.”

Kari Lake, Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Jamaica, also refused to lay the blame at the president’s feet and was one of the few election deniers who continued to boost claims of a stolen election. “America, do you think that our elections are honest? Do you have complete confidence that only legal votes were counted?,” Lake wrote in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

Others, like Harrison Smith, a host on Steve Bannon’s War Room show, turned their ire on their fellow right-wing influencers. He blamed Loomer, Ben Shapiro, Mark Levin, Will Chamberlain, and AIPAC, the prominent lobbying organization, for the losses.

But at least one former Trumpworld figure did take the blame on themselves. Former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem posted on X that the massive losses happened because “we were too successful in the first year of the Trump administration.”

#329. "At Home in Space" opens, caps Air and Space Museum renovation

The Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum has all of its “space” back open.

After seven years of work and nearly $1 billion, the Smithsonian has completed the renovation of the National Air and Space Museum’s flagship building in Washington, DC.

On October 30, the museum debuted its last-to-open spaceflight exhibition, returning “home” with a gallery devoted to establishing a spacefaring civilization.

“Welcome to ‘At Home in Space’!” said curator Jennifer Levasseur, who guided us through a virtual tour of the gallery. “This is the story of long-duration spaceflight in the last few decades. We generally call it ‘reaching orbit.’”

“It’s the prep story, the space shuttle story. It’s what allows us to end up at a place where we have 25-plus years of long-duration spaceflight experience, the capacity for humans to be living in space on the International Space Station (ISS), and then it carries that story forward. So the middle of our story then becomes the ISS, and the end of the story are the next steps,” said Levasseur.

Over the past several years, the National Air and Space Museum has introduced new galleries showcasing how US astronauts first entered space and landed on the Moon (“Destination Moon”); how robotic probes have explored every planet in our solar system (“Kenneth C. Griffin Exploring the Planets”); how technologies and infrastructure impact our daily lives (“RTX Living in the Space Age Hall”), and what approaches spaceflight will take in the years to come (“Futures in Space”).

“At Home in Space,” which follows the similarly themed “Moving Beyond Earth,” immerses guests in the equipment, spacecraft, and orbital platforms that have enabled humanity, from simply visiting space, to living there, setting up the near future for bases on the Moon and Mars.

“We have a great way to attract people into the gallery, which is this overhead mock-up of an astronaut on the end of the robotic arm, and then the backdrop to that is this photo mural—a full-size photo print—of the ISS,” said Levasseur. “Our astronaut up here is intended to be [an actual] person, but I’m not going to share who that is. They are wearing an Expedition 60 patch, so that’ll give you a little clue.”

Some of the gallery’s artifacts include a space shuttle main engine, Robonaut 1A (a prototype humanoid robot), and an extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuit.

“It’s pretty damn special,” said Levasseur of the EMU. “This, as far as I know, is the first and potentially only public display of a fully flown set of EMU equipment in the world. I know NASA has one in its EVA office, but it is not on public display.”

Unlike Apollo-era spacesuits sized to each astronaut, the EMU was designed to be reused, so its components can be swapped out to fit astronauts of different sizes. Introduced during the early years of the space shuttle program, the same EMU suits are still used on the International Space Station for US spacewalks.

The museum’s example is only missing a functioning portable life support system (PLSS), as all the backpacks are still needed for use. So the suit on display only has a PLSS shell for now, according to Levasseur.

The gallery also features Guion Bluford’s and Sally Ride’s in-flight suits, the “shirt-sleeve” outfits the first African American and first US woman wore on the space shuttle (on separate missions).

“Sally is notably missing her jacket, which was a late change to our plan. We were given a drawing of this, a 3D mockup of its display case, and our designers then put it in this way without the jacket on. And we thought, ‘Hey, that’s actually kind of a nice contrast. Let’s keep the jacket out,’” Levasseur told collectSPACE.

The gallery also includes recovered components from the Challenger and Columbia tragedies. It is only the second public display of fallen orbiter debris after a Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex exhibit that opened in Florida in 2015.

“We wanted to honor the individuals who were lost during the shuttle program,” said Levasseur. “So we have an elevon hinge from Challenger that washed up on the beach a few years ago and a little wiring panel fragment from inside the payload bay. And then from Columbia we thought it was appropriate to help tell that story with a piece of RCC [reinforced carbon-carbon]. This is a T-panel from the starboard wing. We also have a CD [compact disc] on a long-term loan from David Brown’s family.”

Visitors can also walk through a full-size mock-up of the space station’s Destiny module, the US national laboratory on the station, and view its equipment on both sides, as well as above and below.

“Originally, the detailing on the floor was going to be a mosaic of real images, but we found that for accessibility reasons people might come in and see the cables and worry that they were real, creating a tripping hazard,” said Levasseur. “On the flip side, and I had to fight to get these, we had to have labels to indicate activity happens on the floor and happens on the overhead. People need to see this is a literally three-dimensional space.”

The module has interactive elements on one side and showcases some of the crew equipment-related artifacts, including coffee cups engineered for use in microgravity.

“This is probably the best section in my mind because it has fun stuff,” said Levasseur, pointing out the flown miniPCR biotech toolkit and MinION portable device used to sequence DNA in space for the first time.

“My absolute favorite thing to work on in this gallery answers the questions: What does space smell like, and what does the ISS smell like? We have little scent oils inside each of these that allow people to smell them,” she said.

Nearby, the first 3D printer used in space is also on display. In 2014, Made In Space (now part of Redwire) and NASA flew the printer, which produced hundreds of objects, from astronaut tools to space station repair parts.

The gallery concludes with a space reserved to exhibit the Artemis I capsule, the spacecraft that flew without astronauts to the Moon in 2022. A Lockheed Martin scale model of Orion holds the place until NASA delivers the real spacecraft to the Smithsonian, which is expected later this year.

“This is the piece of Wright Flyer fabric that went to the Moon with Artemis II, so that’s on display here, too,” Levasseur said, concluding the tour.

The renovation of the National Air and Space Museum also included refacing the exterior cladding, replacing mechanical systems, and other improvements. The first half of the museum reopened in 2022 with eight new or reimagined galleries, the Northrop Grumman Planetarium, a museum store, and the Mars Café. The second phase opened in 2025 with five new galleries, and five additional galleries opened July 1.

Following “At Home in Space,” “Modern Military Aviation” will open on November 11.

“We are thrilled to complete the most extensive project the museum has ever undergone,” Chris Browne, John and Adrienne Mars director of the museum, said in a statement. “With the opening of these last two galleries, the public will once again be able to visit the entirety of the museum and learn from and engage with the nation’s world-class aerospace collection.”

Admission to all of the National Air and Space Museum galleries remains free, but timed-entry passes for the building are required to visit.
